articles.title_orig: Trump-Xi visit to Washington wraps up with few achievements announced
articles.title_zh: Trump-Xi visit to Washington wraps up with few achievements announced
articles.content_orig:
For the last stop of the Chinese leader's state visit, Xi, his wife and the Trumps toured the National Archives briefly on Friday afternoon.
National Archivist Bradford Wilson showed the leaders and their wives the Declaration of Independence and the U.S. Constitution.
Journalists were too far away to hear their conversation, but Mr. Trump did speak briefly to the press.
Asked about his meeting with Xi, the U.S. president said "everything" was accomplished during their meeting, although he didn't elaborate.
During a tea at the White House, Xi thanked the Trumps for the visit.
Through a translator, Xi said everything on their visit was "done to the highest order of perfection" with "thought in every little detail." Xi also said through a translator that he and Mr. Trump "are like two people who are charting the course for the great ship of China-U.S. relations." Xi said they're adding "new substance" to that strategic relationship.
Xi said the two leaders were likely to see each other later this year at the APEC China summit in Shenzhen, and then again at the G20 summit of leaders in the U.S. The G20 is expected to take place at one of Mr. Trump's properties in Miami. Xi welcomed Mr. Trump for a state visit to Beijing in May.
Mr. Trump said he and Xi would be "speaking a lot," adding, "I think our farmers are going to be very happy. A lot of very positive things happened. But America is very happy about this visit and I'm sure China is very happy also. Great things for both countries. And it's been just very, very productive."
The television pool reporter in the room asked Mr. Trump if he asked China to stop sharing intelligence with Iran, but he ignored the question.
David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, told Fox News on Friday that Mr. Trump told Xi it's "unacceptable" for China to be helping Iran in any way with the war. Perdue acknowledged that China has been involved in some assistance that went to Iran directly or indirectly. He also said China has expressed a commitment to not help Iran.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Chinese entities provided satellite images of a base in Jordan to Iran ahead of deadly Iranian strikes that killed three U.S. soldiers and wounded others.
"This has been a continual conversation over some period of time," Perdue told Fox News' Bill Hemmer. "President Xi responded as you might expect. They talked about the U.S. interests. President Trump did a great job making sure that China knows that this is unacceptable. We've seen some movement over the last month as well, but this isn't the first time President Trump has brought it up with President Xi."
Hemmer asked Perdue if that means that China would stop assisting Iran. Perdue said the U.S. has seen "movement" in that direction.
"That's what the commitment is," Perdue responded. "They assured us yesterday they are not doing that. We know that in the past that there was some intel and some potential parts that went to either directly or indirectly. But President Trump again made it very clear, this is unacceptable to us, to have any interaction with Iran with regards to the support of this war."
During remarks at the White House state dinner, Chinese President Xi Jinping said he and President Trump had "sincere and in-depth exchanges" earlier in the day, and "reached common understanding on many issues."
"This has added new substance to the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability," Xi said through a translator.
Xi did not specify what the two leaders discussed or whether they struck any new agreements, but trade and AI were widely believed to be agenda items. The U.S. and China agreed earlier this week to extend a truce on tariffs for two months, forestalling another trade war for now, though the two countries have not struck a broader deal. The two sides are also rivals on advanced AI, with Mr. Trump arguing for light regulations in order to outpace China. Other major pressure points include China's relationships with Iran and Russia and the future of Taiwan.
Xi briefly recounted the history of U.S.-China ties. He pointed to President George Washington's purchase of Chinese porcelain , the two countries' cooperation during World War II and President Richard Nixon's moves to normalize relations with the People's Republic of China.
He said the U.S. and China have come to "another historic juncture," and argued the two countries' ambitions "can surely be mutually reinforcing."
"China and the United States must act as responsible major countries, meet the expectations of our peoples, keep pace with the trend of our times and explore a new approach for major countries to get along with each other," he said.
President Trump gave his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, a large bald eagle sculpture at the end of his brief remarks at Thursday's state dinner.
During a speech recognizing U.S.-China ties, President Trump offered Chinese President Xi Jinping and other guests a "special treat" — a peek at the construction site for the White House ballroom.
"In honor of you, you'll be the first people to step foot on that," the president said, suggesting guests could take a look after the evening's entertainment wraps up.
Mr. Trump speaks about the ballroom frequently, weighing in on design decisions and casting the massive, controversial project as part of his legacy. He has often argued it will allow the White House to host larger state dinners.
"I can tell you that tonight, if we had it, we would've had way more than a thousand people [at the dinner] with standing room only," he said.
In remarks at Thursday's state dinner, President Trump called for the U.S. and China to "continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations."
Mr. Trump, who has long touted his warm personal relationship with Chinese President Xi Jinping, called Xi and his wife "truly outstanding, amazing people."
"As the leaders of our two nations, President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure," Mr. Trump said. "And we've never gotten along better."
Mr. Trump traced the history of U.S.-China relations back to the European explorers who arrived at the American continent while scouring the Atlantic Ocean for new routes to China. He also pointed to early U.S. commercial ties with China, saying the two countries have exchanged "goods, knowledge, customs and ideas."
During a toast to Xi, he said: "May all of our people know a future of harmony, peace and success."
The White House released the invite list for Thursday's state dinner, which includes high-level government officials and several of the world's wealthiest tech executives.
Among the notable people on the guest list are Vice President JD Vance and several Cabinet-level officials: Secretary of State Marco Rubio, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and CIA Director John Ratcliffe.
Mr. Trump's children – Ivanka, Eric and Tiffany – also got invites.
The world's richest person, Elon Musk, is on the list. NVIDIA's Jensen Huang, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Apple's Tim Cook, Google's Sundar Pichai, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Amazon's Jeff Bezos and TikTok investor Jeff Yass also got invites.
Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison is also attending. (Paramount Skydance is the parent company of CBS News.)
President Trump and first lady Melania Trump walked out of the White House's North Portico shortly after 7 p.m. Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, then arrived in a car and posed for photos with the Trumps before walking inside.

articles.title_orig: S&P 500 rises, heads for winning week despite Treasury yield surge: Live updates
articles.title_zh: S&P 500 rises, heads for winning week despite Treasury yield surge: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Treasury yields rose on Friday as recent selling pressure intensified following hawkish Federal Reserve commentary and stronger-than-expected economic data.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note was up more than 4 basis points to 5.209% after reaching its highest rate since June 2007 on Thursday. The 30-year Treasury bond was higher by more than 5 basis points at 5.516% after surging to levels not seen since 2004. The 2-year note yield was up less than 1 basis point at 4.897%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Investors also weighed a global bond sell-off this week as Japanese government bonds, U.K. gilts, German bunds and other eurozone bonds hit fresh highs. Eurozone and Japanese government bond yields edged lower on Friday.
Treasury yields have been driven higher by hawkish comments from Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr, who said in a speech on Wednesday that "further policy adjustments" can be expected to bring inflation down to target. Other factors included stubbornly high oil prices and the purchasing managers' index report hitting its highest level in more than four years.
Traders were last pricing in a 66% chance of a rate hike in October, according to the CME FedWatch tool .
"Ahead, we think that there are enough rate hike fears discounted at this juncture, and certainly enough to take care of perceived inflation risks," ING's regional head of research for the Americas Padhraic Garvey and senior rates strategist Benjamin Schroeder wrote in a note on Friday.
"But, government bond yields are primed to remain under pressure on a pure debt dynamic theory, which translates into pressure for some re-widening in swap spreads, and especially in the 10yr area."
On Friday, durable goods orders in August came in relatively unchanged , while economists polled by Dow Jones had expected a decline of 0.3%. Additionally, consumer sentiment plummeted in September.

articles.title_orig: The Supreme Court revives a controversial data system for citizenship checks
articles.title_zh: The Supreme Court revives a controversial data system for citizenship checks
articles.content_orig:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin speaks during a news conference July 1 in New York. David Delgado/AP hide caption
The U.S. Supreme Court has for now revived a federal data system the Department of Homeland Security revamped into a tool to check the citizenship of millions of Americans on state voter rolls. The tool has mistakenly flagged some eligible voters as potential noncitizens.
The news comes as the Trump administration has been pouring resources into searching for noncitizens on voter rolls ahead of the upcoming election.
Many states uploaded their voter lists to the expanded version of the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements data system — known as SAVE — sharing that voter information with the federal government. Tens of millions of voter records were run through SAVE before it was blocked by a federal judge in June.
The Supreme Court's decision clears the way for the administration to again use the revamped SAVE in its hunt for noncitizens on voter rolls, as well as in its unprecedented project of compiling lists of adult citizens in each state .
Any impact on the midterm elections is unclear. Federal law bans states from "systematically" removing voters from rolls within 90 days of a federal election.
The Trump administration and Republican state officials have argued that statute should not apply to removing noncitizens who were improperly registered. And the federal government argued to the Supreme Court that at a minimum, the updated SAVE should be able to be used for individual removal decisions ahead of an election.
In siding with the Trump administration, the court's majority wrote that the lower court order that halted the expanded SAVE prevents the federal government "from using the modified SAVE program to conduct individualized inquiries, which are permitted under federal law during this [90-day] period. The District Court's order thus inhibits the Federal Government's efforts to assist state and local agencies in the proper administration of the midterm elections."
The Supreme Court's three liberal justices dissented from the ruling, and would have denied the Trump administration's stay application.
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson authored the dissent, writing about the "majority's omission of any consideration of the harms that might occur if the modified SAVE system is allowed to continue operating. The District Court highlighted such harms, noting the risk that States might cancel the voter registrations of at least some recently naturalized citizens or force such persons to provide proof of citizenship before voting."
SAVE is a 40-year-old federal data system that was created to check the immigration status of noncitizens to determine their eligibility for public benefits.
Then, DHS overhauled SAVE last year by linking it for the first time with Social Security Administration records, which include most Americans. The overhaul also allowed bulk queries to SAVE, and DHS encouraged states to upload their entire voter rolls to SAVE to verify those registered are U.S. citizens and not listed as deceased in federal records.
In June, U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan, a Biden appointee, blocked use of the modified version of SAVE , finding that its aggregation and disclosure of sensitive data violated the Social Security Act, the Privacy Act and the Administrative Procedures Act.
"The federal government has knowingly trampled on the privacy rights of American citizens in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote," she wrote.
After an appeals court panel refused to stay the lower court's decision in a 2-1 vote, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer appealed to the Supreme Court earlier this month .
In his appeal, Sauer wrote that since May 2025, the updated version of SAVE has verified more than 65 million voters across 26 states, and has flagged 28,635 as potential noncitizens.
"The district court's order, however, makes it harder to detect ineligible voters, undermining the integrity of federal elections and public confidence in the results of those elections," he wrote.
The League of Women Voters and the Electronic Privacy Information Center, which first challenged the legality of the SAVE overhaul a year ago, argued in a brief to the Supreme Court that Congress has not authorized the federal government to create a "master database of U.S. Citizens," nor does it have data that could do that accurately. The brief added that multiple statutes restrict repurposing and sharing Americans' sensitive data.
"Disregarding these laws, the government has recklessly created an error-laden master citizenship database that endangers millions of Americans' privacy and voting rights," the groups wrote.
They wrote that even though 65 million voters had been verified by the revamped SAVE, the government had not yet released the system's error rate, or how many Americans' citizenship was misrepresented "and who consequently have been forced to reverify their citizenship to retain their voter registration or obtain government benefits."
Even though Election Day is just over a month away and voting is underway, the Trump administration could try to make use of the expanded version of SAVE right away in its quest to check registered voters' citizenship.
An executive order President Trump signed in March calls for federal agencies to consult SAVE data, along with other federal records, to create state-by-state lists of adult U.S. citizens. The same order directs the U.S. attorney general to prioritize investigating and prosecuting election officials who provide ballots to ineligible voters. Even though the executive order says such state lists are to be completed 60 days before an election and that deadline has already passed, federal officials have indicated the project is still underway – although it is facing a legal challenge.
Eligible voters have been erroneously flagged by SAVE, which has been unable to confirm the citizenship of certain categories of foreign-born people who become U.S. citizens.
After Texas ran its entire voter list of 18 million voters through SAVE, the system flagged 2,724 voters as potential noncitizens. County election officials then gave those individuals 30 days to prove their citizenship and, following state law, removed anyone who did not respond in time.
As NPR first reported in December , that effort resulted in citizens being removed from the rolls. Anthony Nel, whose story NPR highlighted in that reporting, gave a declaration in this lawsuit.
A recent press release from the Texas secretary of state revealed that of the 2,724 voters that were initially flagged by SAVE as potential noncitizens, some 20% were later found to be citizens who were reinstated. The same release said the office referred 117 cases identified by SAVE, or 4.2% of those flagged, for investigation for possible noncitizen voting.

articles.title_orig: Man City refuse to deny guilty verdicts in Premier League 115 breaches case - sources
articles.title_zh: Man City refuse to deny guilty verdicts in Premier League 115 breaches case - sources
articles.content_orig:
Manchester City have been found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges the club has faced regarding breaching Premier League financial rules, according a report in The Athletic.
The sanctions have not yet been decided, and City are expected to appeal, according to an article by The Athletic’s David Ornstein on Friday, who cited anonymous sources briefed on the matter.
Sanctions could include points deductions, financial penalties, and even stripping titles won by City and relegation from the Premier League.
A spokesperson for City, who have denied the charges, said, “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such, Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023.
“The club have diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”
Since a 2008 takeover by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the United Arab Emirates royal family, City have been transformed from also-rans into the Premier League’s dominant force.
Eight of the club’s 10 league titles have come in the past 15 seasons, plus a first and only Champions League in 2023.
The club has been accused of breaching financial rules while on the rise to their current status.
Of the 115 charges, 80 are for breaches of regulations from 2009 to 2018, while the remaining 35 relate to failing to cooperate with the Premier League’s investigation.
The charges stem from leaked documents published by the German news magazine Der Spiegel in 2018.
Emails purportedly sent between top City executives showed the club had inflated sponsorship revenue from the UAE state-controlled airline Etihad and telecommunications firm Etisalat by disguising direct investment from Mansour’s Abu Dhabi United Group as income.
Other documents claimed to show off-the-books payments to then-manager Roberto Mancini via consultancy fees from a club in Abu Dhabi.
City have insisted there is a “comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence” to prove its innocence.
They have already defended their position in one case in which a two-year ban from the Champions League by UEFA was overturned by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) in 2020.
The CAS found most of the alleged breaches of overstating sponsorship revenue were either not established or “time-barred” because they fell outside the five-year statutory limit for prosecution.
But no such time limitation clause exists in the Premier League case.
Everton and Nottingham Forest were both hit by points deductions in the 2023/24 season for single breaches of profit and sustainability rules.
A severe punishment would also raise doubts about the future of City’s cast of star players, including prolific striker Erling Haaland.
Other clubs could make a claim for titles to be stripped and compensation if City gained an unfair advantage by proscribed means.

articles.title_orig: Ed Sheeran's Gillette Stadium concerts canceled due to nor'easter, tour promoter says
articles.title_zh: Ed Sheeran's Gillette Stadium concerts canceled due to nor'easter, tour promoter says
articles.content_orig:
Ed Sheeran’s concerts scheduled for this weekend at Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts have been canceled due to severe weather, amid wider turmoil surrounding the British pop star’s tour.
The concerts scheduled for Friday and Saturday at the New England Patriots home stadium were scrapped because of the upcoming nor’easter , Messina Touring, Sheeran’s touring group, said in an Instagram statement.
“Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, we have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium,” the statement said. “The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority.”
The touring group said that refunds are available and that ticket holders who purchased through Ticketmaster will be automatically refunded.
The announcement comes amid a wider scandal for Sheeran’s “Loop” tour since one of its opening acts was forced out for voicing pro-Palestinian views.
Earlier this month, rapper Macklemore said he was removed from Sheeran’s tour after speaking out in support for the Palestinian people at the tour’s shows in New Jersey. Macklemore said he was removed at the behest of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft and alleged that Kraft organized a boycott among stadium owners.
Kraft did not immediately return a request for comment. In a previous statement he said he did not intend to stifle Palestinian support but to ensure a “welcoming environment” at Gillette Stadium.
Macklemore’s removal prompted Sheeran’s other opening acts — Aaron Rowe, Lukas Graham, Finneas and his house band, Beoga — to withdraw in protest.
A rep for Sheeran did not immediately return a request for comment. In his first concert since the scandal, Sheeran apologized for the scenario.
“I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician,” Sheeran said, “but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet.”
On Thursday, Macklemore announced a Free Palestine Tour for this fall.
The multiday nor’easter is expected to hit the East Coast, affecting states from Virginia to Rhode Island. Coastal flood alerts are in effect for 33 million people. Wind gusts are expected to peak on Saturday, reaching up to 60 mph in coastal locations.
I’m a reporter on NBC News’ breaking news team, covering crime, extreme weather, pop culture and more. I recently covered Hurricane Milton, which devastated the Tampa, Florida, metropolitan area, and the student-led protests at Columbia University.

articles.title_orig: Man shot during 2024 Trump campaign rally in Butler dies
articles.title_zh: Man shot during 2024 Trump campaign rally in Butler dies
articles.content_orig:
Copenhaver was one of three Trump rally attendees who was shot, as well as Trump, whose ear was grazed by a bullet
One of the three attendees who was shot at Donald Trump's 2024 presidential campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, has passed away from complications stemming from his injuries, according to the Pennsylvania attorney general.
Jim Copenhaver, 76, was struck twice when a gunman opened fire from a nearby rooftop. Another attendee, Corey Comperatore, was killed in the shooting and Trump's ear was grazed by a bullet.
Copenhaver died on Wednesday at a hospital in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, according to a statement from the Allegheny County medical examiner shared with local media.
The gunman, 20-year-old Thomas Crooks, was killed by Secret Service after he opened fire.
Months on, Trump shooting witness still stunned by security lapse
In a post on his social media site Truth Social, Trump called Copenhaver a "true American patriot".
"More than two years ago in Butler, Pennsylvania, a crazed gunman attempted to stifle our America First Movement. Instead, Jim and so many other wonderful Patriots who love our Country, stood united in defense of our shared values of Freedom, Liberty, and Justice," Trump said. "Our hearts and prayers are with the Copenhaver family, especially his incredible wife Marianne."
An attorney for Copenhaver's family said his dedication to the US was a "defining part of his life".
"As a veteran, he proudly served our nation in the armed forces, and his love of country never wavered," the lawyer said in a statement to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
In an interview with CBS a year after the Butler rally, Copenhaver and David Dutch, the third attendee who was shot, said they had been through infections and surgeries after being wounded.
Copenhaver was shot in the arm and the abdomen. A year later, the bullet was still lodged in his body next to his spine, he told CBS, causing him to walk with a cane.
Both Dutch and Copenhaver sued the federal government for damages in June, arguing the Secret Service failed to ensure their safety and was therefore liable for their injuries.
Republicans in the US House of Representatives also paid tribute to Copenhaver on Friday, saying in a social media post: "Jim endured unimaginable hardship with strength and perseverance."

articles.title_orig: Winners and losers from Packers' Thursday Night Football dud vs. Falcons
articles.title_zh: Winners and losers from Packers' Thursday Night Football dud vs. Falcons
articles.content_orig:
The Atlanta Falcons played like a rejuvenated team that finally had its quarterback back . The Green Bay Packers had the look of an undermanned squad still asking too much of its own quarterback.
That pretty much summed up an ugly Thursday night game in Wisconsin, the Falcons steamrolling the Packers 35-14 for their first win of the season as QB Michael Penix Jr. made his 2026 debut. Atlanta, which had 16 points all season entering the game, rolled off 27 in a row at one point in a runaway that immediately restored them to relevance in the NFC South. The Pack, meanwhile − still without injured superstar OLB Micah Parsons and Pro Bowl RB Josh Jacobs, among others − moved into the basement of the NFC North with a 1-2 record that somehow seems far more problematic than Atlanta’s.
The scoreboard said plenty, but there were quite a few other winners and losers Thursday, and they are as follows:
The Falcons quarterback, and team’s highly scrutinized first-round pick from 2024, started his first game in nearly a year after sufficiently recovering from the third ACL reconstruction of his football career, dating back to his college days. He threw an interception while getting reacclimated on his first drive, but ultimately completed 18 of 25 throws for 256 yards and a TD. His connection with WR Drake London certainly seemed fully intact, the duo hooking up nine times for 194 yards. Playing on a Thursday night also confers another benefit to Penix, who now gets 11 days to recover and gauge how his body responds with Atlanta scheduled to next play Oct. 5 in New Orleans, Week 4’s Monday nighter.
In the depths of their 0-2 start , the Falcons entered the game with nary a touchdown in the previous seven quarters – and just one all season – and had not played a snap in the opposition red-zone in 2026, a dry spell no team had experienced through its first two games since 2008. Thursday, they scored four touchdowns in five visits inside Green Bay's 20-yard line.
Y’all remember he’s a two-time NFL Coach of the Year, right? That seems to get obscured a bit after the rocky end to his six-year tenure with the Cleveland Browns – where all tenures end rockily – and was certainly accentuated by Atlanta’s ghastly start to this season. But if Penix didn’t completely unlock Stefanski’s offense, which did rack up a gaudy 498 yards, he certainly stabilized it and provided ample hope that the Falcons could still be a contender for the divisional throne this season. After notching his first win as Atlanta's HC, Stefanski is also now 6-0 on Thursday nights … 41-60 (playoffs included) during the rest of the week.
Maybe the lone silver lining for the Green and Gold, the fifth-year receiver continues to show what he's capable of when healthy, which has been the biggest obstacle to date during his career. Watson's first-quarter TD catch, which staked Green Bay to an early lead, was his fourth of the season, tying him for the league lead − albeit with one more game under his belt than Seattle's Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Detroit's Amon-Ra St. Brown.
It's been a rough year-plus for the Atlanta defensive coordinator, even more so off the field than on. In 2025, Ulbrich's son infamously prank-called then-Colorado QB Shedeur Sanders as he tumbled into the third day of the draft, embarrassing the family and lightening the coach's wallet. This year has been much worse, Ulbrich's wife losing her battle with cancer in July. An inspired defensive effort against the Packers − and with the Falcons down several key starters due to injuries and pass rusher James Pearce Jr.'s suspension − only counts for so much, but it's nice to see something go right for the NFL lifer given all he's been through on a personal level.
As you’d expect, Bijan Robinson provided plenty of mustard to the Falcons offense, rushing for 194 yards and two scores. However he also got some nice backup from RB2 Brian Robinson Jr. (no relation), who chipped in with 50 yards and a score of his own.
Boy, do the Packers miss Jacobs – to say nothing of the legitimacy he provides to the play-action approach coach Matt LaFleur favored in 2025, a strategy that was obviously dead in the water against Atlanta ... yet curiously employed on fourth-and-1 from the Falcons' 7-yard line on the Packers' first possession of the second half. (The play failed miserably.) After averaging a meager 64.5 yards on the ground in their first two games, the Pack were far more ineffectual Thursday – producing all of 17 yards, among the lowest totals in the storied franchise's history. And with no return in sight for Jacobs, who remains on the commissioner’s exempt list – not to mention a battered O-line that was missing LG Aaron Banks and RT Zach Bako-Bewele, who’s out for the season with a knee injury – little reason to believe matters will improve any time soon.
The leader of the Pack on the field and at the bank – with a contract averaging $55 million annually – Love understandably continues to struggle trying to operate an offense that’s completely out of kilter while attempting to compensate for a defense that’s been grated for at least 35 points twice in three weeks. Aside from the lopsided pass-run ratio (54 dropbacks vs. nine rushes on Thursday), Love was also navigating his new blocking combination without injured WR Jayden Reed. While his position and paycheck put the onus on him, Love, who’s barely completing 50% of his passes this season − despite 312 empty-calorie yards and two TDs through the air Thursday − continues to be stuck in what’s presently a very unenviable position.
"I think a lot of areas we need to improve. But at the end of the day, I'll just sit here and look at myself and say there's so much stuff I can improve on to make us as an offense better," Love said afterward. "It always starts with me. To be the leader of the team, I've got to improve and be better in a lot of areas. There's a lot of stuff that I'll look at on film that I won't be happy with how I performed tonight."
There shouldn't be too much blame assessed to the Packers pass rusher. But we can't ignore that his roughing penalty on Penix late in the first quarter − when the Packers were leading 7-0 − kept the Falcons on the field following what appeared to be a failed third down. Bijan Robinson escaped for a 55-yard run on the next play, was in the end zone two snaps later, and the Falcons never looked back. Oops.
If you took the Falcons' Kyle Pitts or Packers' Tucker Kraft with an early pick in your fantasy draft ... bummer. They've combined for 11 receptions, none for TDs ... all season.
Unless Penix gets reinjured − sadly, his history suggests it will happen − the Dolphins castoff ain't playing extensively here. Expected to start in Week 1 before he injured an oblique muscle in practice , Tagovailoa's best bet to rekindle his career in 2026 might entail a release from his one-year deal or a trade to a quarterback-needy team, say the New York Giants potentially?
Arguably the most iconic stadium in the NFL , it’s been privy to a lot of good football in recent decades – and most certainly on opening night. But not Thursday. The loss to the previously winless and inept Falcons was not only embarrassing and frustrating for the locals, it also ended the Packers’ streak of winning 13 consecutive home openers.

articles.title_zh: Nor’easter Could Bring Heavy Rain, Winds, and Flooding to East Coast
articles.content_orig:
An early-season nor'easter will bring coastal flooding, high surf, strong winds and rain to parts of the East Coast through the weekend, with impacts from North Carolina to New England.
New York City and especially Boston need to stay weather aware this weekend, and prepare the same as you would for a tropical storm.
The nor'easter is strengthening as it heads north. The map below shows the winds and rain as the low moves north along the East Coast.
Wind gusts over 30 mph, with occasional gusts from 40 to 50 mph, are occurring along the coast from southeast New England to the Outer Banks of North Carolina.
( MORE: Nor'easter tracking maps )
Coastal flooding is also occurring at high tide from parts of Long Island to North Carolina.

Here's a general timeline of the storm and its impacts over the next several days.
The map below shows coastal flood alerts have been issued by the National Weather Service. These alerts include Atlantic City, Long Island, the Norfolk metro area, Ocean City (Maryland and New Jersey), downtown Boston, Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket.
The most significant coastal flooding will be from the northern Outer Banks of North Carolina to the  Jersey shore, including the Virginia Tidewater, as well as Chesapeake Bay and Delaware Bay.
(WATCH: Nor'easter waves slam stilt homes on the Outer Banks )
This flooding will happen for multiple high tides into the weekend, in these areas. It will also be boosted by Saturday's full moon, with some of the highest astronomical tides of the month.
Given this repeated battering from high surf, beach erosion is expected along stretches of these beaches, potentially reaching extreme levels for some areas.
At least minor coastal high tide flooding will also develop in parts of New England by late Friday into the weekend.
One bit of good fortune with this storm is that its rainfall will be spread out over several days, rather than arriving in one short deluge.
While we expect the most rain to fall from southern New England to New Jersey, those rainfall totals in the map below will be stretched out through Monday.
That means any rainfall flooding should be mainly local in nature in some of the traditional urban trouble spots.
That rainfall could also add to any coastal flooding at high tide through Sunday.
In the New York City metro area, the heaviest rainfall is expected in Long Island, with less rain as you go west into the outer New Jersey suburbs.
High wind warnings are in effect for parts of southeast New England, including Boston and Providence, and also along coasts of Delaware and New Jersey. In these areas, gusts up to 60 mph are possible through Saturday night.
In these areas, some tree damage and power outages are most likely. Ground soaked from the nor'easter's rain, as well as trees still with leaves will only enhance this threat of tree damage and outages.
Otherwise, occasional gusts from 40 to 50 mph are possible from North Carolina's Outer Banks to other parts of coastal New England. Some sporadic power outages and tree limb damage are also possible in these areas.

( MORE: Nor'easter impacts on Major League Baseball's weekend )
Some gusts topped 40 mph along the coast from southern Massachusetts down to the Virginia Tidewater Wednesday.
And those persistent winds are piled up water from the ocean and bays along parts of the coast.
Minor to moderate coastal flooding was reported from parts of the Jersey Shore to southeast Virginia during Wednesday's morning and evening high tides.
Flooding was reported Wednesday morning in downtown Norfolk, Smithfield and Suffolk, Virginia, according to the National Weather Service.
Widespread gusts of 30-45 mph were ongoing as of Thursday evening, with peak gusts over 45 mph reported along the coast of North Carolina.
Those persistent winds were piling up water from the ocean and bays along parts of the coast. Water levels reached major flood stage during high tide Thursday evening.
A 16-mile stretch of the North Carolina Highway 12 on the Outer Banks is closed in both directions due to ocean overwash. Specifically, the road is closed from Sea Oats Drive to Oregon Inlet Road in Dare County.
Rising waters forced the cancellation of the Oceans Calling festival in Maryland.
You might think it is too early for a nor’easter, but the criteria for a nor’easter are met more often than you would think.
A nor’easter simply means that the winds blow into an area from the northeast. For the Northeast, that usually means an area of low pressure is just off the coast, which brings the winds in this direction.
(More: What is a nor’easter? )
Most people usually think of snow and ice with nor’easters and that is because nor’easters do tend to occur more in the late fall and winter.
The most notable nor’easters tend to bring heavy snow because these lows move up along the Gulf Stream, tapping into the warm ocean. This warm, moist air then clashes with the cold air over the Northeast to create heavy snowfall. Fortunately, this one is occurring way earlier, so it is all rain this time.

The New York City Council is readying legislation to rein in the artificial intelligence industry as AI companies continue to grow their presence in the city.
One bill will ban businesses from selling or deploying AI systems in the city unless an independent inspector certified they met city standards for data quality, bias, privacy and security, Fortune reported Friday morning.
That bill will also require AI labs to engineer a "kill switch," i.e. a human override to shut down a model or agent in the event it goes rogue.
Failing to comply with these regulations will lead to $25,000 fines per violation, City Council Speaker Julie Menin told Fortune in an interview. Since the penalties would be assessed for each AI agent involved, the total fines could be substantial.
Another piece of legislation will reward whistleblowers with a portion of the fines collected from AI firms who break the law, Fortune reported.
The new regulations are expected to be introduced on Friday ahead of an Oct. 5 Committee of the Whole hearing with all 51 council members in attendance.
Pope Leo XIV warned Friday that a "paradise of machines" could pose a risk to humanity during the opening to his four-day trip in France .
In a speech at the Élysée Palace, the pope said it was an urgent concern of his that "we do not lose our humanity amid the paradise of machines that are invading and conditioning our daily lives," according to the Guardian.
The phrase "paradise of machines" is a reference to Georges Bernanos’s 1947 essay "France Against the Robots," in which he argued that industrialization and technological advancement was contributing to the dulling of the human spirit and mass loneliness.
Pope Leo has made artificial intelligence one of the defining issues of his papacy, creating a commission within the Vatican in May to address the growing ethical concerns with AI.
"Technology should not be considered, in itself, as a force antagonistic to humanity," Pope Leo wrote in his May 2026 encyclical Magnifica Humanitas. "At the same time, each phase of progress has also revealed the ambiguity of tools that can cause harm when not oriented toward the good."
A federal appeals court ruled Friday that the Trump administration is allowed to exclude Anthropic from being considered for all U.S. military contracts.
In a 2-1 ruling, the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals found that Pentagon acted lawfully when it removed Anthropic's Claude AI from its supply chain.
The court argued that the company's ability to restrict how its models performed on certain "lawful" military tasks constituted a national security risk under federal law.
Back in February, the Pentagon claimed Anthropic had asked whether its product was used in the January military operation to capture Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro, Fox News Digital reported at the time.
Sources told Fox News Digital that Anthropic posed this question in a way that suggested it may not approve of its potential involvement in the Maduro operation.
The relationship between the Department of War and Anthropic deteriorated further when CEO Dario Amodei put out a blog post on Feb. 26, saying he would not allow Claude to be used for "mass domestic surveillance" or "fully autonomous weapons."
"Anthropic understands that the Department of War, not private companies, makes military decisions," Amodei wrote. "However, in a narrow set of cases, we believe AI can undermine, rather than defend, democratic values."
Shortly after Amodei's statement was released, War Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that the federal government would cease using all of Anthropic's technology.
"Our position has never wavered and will never waver: the Department of War must have full, unrestricted access to Anthropic’s models for every LAWFUL purpose in defense of the Republic," Hegseth wrote in a post on X at the time. "Cloaked in the sanctimonious rhetoric of 'effective altruism,' they have attempted to strong-arm the United States military into submission."
Jason Calacanis, an angel investor and Dotcom era startup founder, put out a cryptic social media post advising SpaceX and Meta to release "an iPhone competitor with no apps — just agents and optimized for local AI and privacy."
His post on X included a screenshot of an iPhone dock showing just two apps: xAI's Grok Bot and Meta's Muse, two advanced AI agent systems designed to automate complex work tasks.
It's not entirely clear what Calacanis is envisioning, but Meta has already waded into introducing hardware paired with its AI software.
This week, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg introduced the Muse Charm, a pocket-watch-sized device that would have the Muse AI agent system included.
"We packed the whole Muse experience, including the whole real-time voice and avatar stack, into something that fits on a keychain and is always available to talk to," Zuckerberg said at this year's Meta Connect event.
If the gadget were to catch on, users would not need to access Muse via a smartphone from Apple or Google, potentially cutting into those companies' profit margins. The Muse Charm is expected to roll out sometime in December.
Pope Leo XIV’s cardinal who leads an artificial intelligence commission within the Vatican admitted on a Politico podcast that he doesn't use AI.
Cardinal Michael Czerny told the Brussels Playbook Podcast that he hasn't had the time to start using it in his daily work, even though the pope appointed him to chair the Vatican’s Inter-Dicasterial Commission on Artificial Intelligence four months ago.
“I’m quite willing and happy to learn,” Czerny said. “I feel it’s my moral duty also to use it so that I have personal experience, and I hope it helps me with my work.”
Czerny has called on European politicians to heed warnings about frontier AI models breaking free of human oversight.
Chinese AI startup DeepSeek has hit an annualized revenue run rate of $1 billion, more than double what it was a few months ago, The Information reported.
An annualized revenue run rate estimates how much money a company would make in a year if it continued earning at its current pace.
DeepSeek stunned Silicon Valley last year when its AI models proved competitive with leading offerings from OpenAI and Anthropic, despite being developed with far fewer resources.
Reuters reported earlier this month that DeepSeek is planning to go public domestically to fund its expansion.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Wednesday that companies developing advanced artificial intelligence models do not need to work together to prevent the catastrophic outcomes that many industry leaders have warned about.
In an interview with former Wall Street Journal columnist Joanna Stern, Zuckerberg also cast doubt on the mores alarmist members of the AI sector, some of whom have said human extinction is possibility if AI improves without guardrails in place.
"I think that there's a lot of rhetoric that is filled with doom, and my view on this is that there are a number of labs that are working on building advanced AI, and I don't think that we need some kind of  industry-wide coordination to not necessarily mess this up," he said on Stern's show "New Things."
"I think that just each lab needs to take the time, and when it sees that there are issues, you just take the time that you need internally to make sure that you're proceeding safely," Zuckerberg added.
Meta launched its personal AI assistant, Muse, on Sept. 8 in the United States. It's available on major app stores and has been integrated into Meta's Ray Ban audio glasses.
Elon Musk is making a sky-high prediction for artificial intelligence. The SpaceX CEO says computing will eventually move almost entirely off Earth.
“The amount of compute in space will obviously round up to 100% of all compute,” Musk wrote on X in response to a video about Google’s Project Suncatcher.

Oooh, that unmatched satisfaction of peeling a perfectly printed label or sticker and slapping it on your water bottle, food container or whatever else is close by! If anyone knows what I'm talking about, this one's for you – the crafting giant Cricut is taking the joy of label and high-end sticker making to the next level with two new machines: the Cricut StickerPix Print and the Cricut StickerPix Print + Cut .
Available now, both models could easily hit our lists of the best label makers , or the best laminators . But they're so much more than that. They serve as compact mini-print shops that print and laminate pro-quality, water- and scratch-resistant stickers and photos using ultra-vivid 300 DPI dye-sublimation technology.
That may be a mouthful, but it basically means these are very capable little things. The standard Cricut StickerPix Print (£159.99 for the Essential Bundle) works seamlessly with pre-cut sticker sheets—perfect for quick, uniform labels. Meanwhile, the advanced Cricut StickerPix Print + Cut (£249.99 for the Essential Bundle) adds a built-in cutter, automatically kiss-cutting custom shapes directly around your unique designs. Both connect effortlessly to the free Cricut Design Space app, meaning you can transform your smartphone photos and designs into tactile stickers in minutes.
The Cricut StickerPix Print Essential Bundle has everything you'll need. It includes the machine, an ink cartridge (54 prints), 18 circle pre-cut sticker sheets, 18 rectangle pre-cut sticker sheets, 18 glossy photo papers, a power adapter, and a material tray. Perfect for beginner crafters.
At $299, the Cricut StickerPix Print + Cut Essential Bundle equips you for custom sticker projects instantly. Included alongside the machine is an ink cartridge (36 prints), 18 glossy sticker sheets, 18 photo paper sheets, a pre-installed cutting tool, material tray, power adapter, and a free Cricut Access trial subscription.
So, who's this for? Well, everyone from label/sticker homebody maniacs to digital artists and small business owners.
If you run a market stall or Etsy shop, the StickerPix Print could be a really nice addition to your business. It’s efficient for batch-printing logos, price tags, QR codes, or packaging seals using the pre-cut circular and rectangular sheets. And, because the dye-sublimation prints come out completely dry and laminated, you won't have to worry about smudging labels. It's also ideal for anyone who wants to label their spice jars or craft room storage without fussing over intricate cuts.
I think there's also scope for illustrators to use these things, especially those who want to share their art at conventions – after all, everyone loves stickers! You can upload a hand-drawn illustration or a photo from your phone, and the machine will print, laminate, and precisely kiss-cut a custom border around the image so the backing stays intact for easy peeling.
For me, I'm excited to use them to create unique water bottle sticks and fun gifts for my son's birthday party bags.
Looking around at the other sticker makers in this price range, I think Cricut has successfully bridged the gap between a pro print shop and an everyday crafting tool. I can't wait to get my hands on them to fully try them out.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo XIV begins historic 4-day visit to France
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo XIV begins historic 4-day visit to France
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo arrived in France on Friday, Sept. 25, starting a four-day tour across Paris, Lourdes, and Metz that includes speeches and a massive outdoor mass. (HOST BROADCASTER via Reuters.)
Pope Leo XIV began his visit to France on Friday for his fifth Apostolic Journey as Pontiff. The four-day trip marks the first formal papal visit to the country once called "the eldest daughter of the Church" since Pope Benedict XVI’s visit in September 2008.
French bishops announced the visit’s theme as "That the world may have life," and it comes as the officially secular nation is seeing an influx of new baptisms. So far this year, according to the Conference of Bishops of France, more than 21,000 adults have joined the Church, an increase driven by 18 to 25-year-olds.
"Pope Leo's visit to France has sparked a real tidal wave" of interest, retired French Bishop Marc Stenger told Reuters. "French Catholics are… saying ​loudly that they need the Church to find their way in these uncertain moments in world history."
POPE LEO WARNS AI RISKS BECOMING TOOL OF 'DOMINATION, EXCLUSION AND DEATH' IN NEW ENCYCLICAL
The pope will visit Metz on Sept. 28, 2026 to conclude his four-day state and pastoral trip to France, which also includes stops in Paris and Lourdes. (Jean-Christophe Verhaegen / AFP via Getty Images)
The rise comes after a 2021 report found that some 330,000 French children had been abused by Catholic clergy and lay leaders over seven decades, and said the Church had shown "deep, total and even cruel indifference" ​to victims. Stenger, who led the Diocese of Troyes from 1999 to 2020, told Reuters the scandals "have deeply wounded the Church and damaged its credibility."
In what is described as an unusual move, the Vatican press office announced Pope Leo will meet privately in Lourdes with seven of those victims as part of a message of healing and vulnerability.
SAN FRANCISCO ARCHDIOCESE AGREES TO $395M SETTLEMENT WITH 530 CLERGY ABUSE SURVIVORS
The Vatican calls the trip, "a journey that unites faith and public engagement, memory and the future, with listening and bridge-building at its heart." After being greeted by French President Emmanuel Macron and a courtesy visit to Élysée Palace on Friday, Pope Leo is scheduled to make 15 speeches during his visit. He is expected to speak on several spiritual and societal themes, including the need to protect immigrants , the sick and unborn, and defend human dignity in the era of AI, and address themes of peace, culture, and unity.
President of France Emmanuel Macron and First Lady Brigitte Macron welcome Pope Leo XIV to Élysée Palace on Sept. 25, 2026 in Paris, France. (Tom Nicholson/Getty Images)
French bishops have expressed surprise at the level of interest in the visit. The Associated Press reports organizers for Pope Leo’s Saturday Mass at Paris’ Place de la Concorde, expecting up to 1 million people, have lengthened the security perimeter, extending the site beyond the 1.2-mile length of the Champs-Élysées, where Pope Leo will parade in the Popemobile.
Among his more noteworthy stops, Pope Leo will worship and speak on Sunday at the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes, one of Christianity’s most-visited pilgrimage destinations, especially popular with the sick. It is where an ailing Pope John Paul II , on his final foreign trip in 2004, delivered a forceful condemnation of abortion and euthanasia.
Pope Leo XIV attends the Welcome Ceremony at Paris Orly International Airport on Sept. 25, 2026 in Paris, France. (Simone Risoluti - Vatican Media via Vatican Pool/Getty Images)
Pope Leo’s visit, however, comes after France’s recent national debate and subsequent passage of legislation allowing adults with incurable illnesses to receive lethal medication. That followed 2024 legislation enshrining abortion as a constitutional right .
POPE LEO PROMOTES ARCHBISHOP WHO BARRED PELOSI FROM COMMUNION TO ONE OF VATICAN'S HIGHEST COURTS
On Friday, Pope Leo will speak at the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, or UNESCO, headquarters in Paris. Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni says Leo will likely reiterate his call for an AI slowdown and speak "with regard to the meaning of existence, to what makes human beings human and what does not."
The speech comes after the Pope’s May manifesto in which Leo warned of the dangers of AI and urged international regulation of the industry. His position again puts him at odds with President Trump, who has encouraged AI innovation so the U.S. can compete with and surpass China.
A crucifix stands in front of the Basilique Notre-Dame du Rosaire, its spire draped with a banner marking the upcoming visit of Pope Leo XIV, five days ahead of the pontiff's trip to the site as part of his apostolic journey to France, in Lourdes on Sept. 22, 2026.
Following his UNESCO visit, Pope Leo holds a prayer service at the newly-restored Cathedral of Notre-Dame, marking the first papal visit since a 2019 fire nearly destroyed one of France’s national landmarks.
He concludes his trip on Monday with a symbolic full-day visit to the border city of Metz, the birthplace of former French Prime Minister Robert Schuman, considered one of the founding fathers of the European Union. It is a backdrop the Vatican says the Pope will use to "champion friendship among European peoples."

French Ambassador to the Vatican Charles Personnaz told Reuters that Macron has invited leaders from all 27 EU members to attend the speech and meet with the Pontiff. Other media reports say Ukrainian President V olodymyr Zelenskyy may also attend.

articles.title_orig: The drones Russia could strike Europe with from Mediterranean fleet
articles.title_zh: The drones Russia could strike Europe with from Mediterranean fleet
articles.content_orig:
After more than four years of war between Russia and Ukraine, technology and spending on military equipment have evolved significantly.
A number of Russian drones have been detected flying over European Union territory. There have been incursions into Poland and Bulgaria although, according to a CIA report, the situation could become more complicated.
The latest information from the CIA has made it clear that there is a risk of Russian drone attacks on Spain, France or Italy launched from containers on ships belonging to the shadow fleet in the Mediterranean. So, what kind of drones is the Russian army using? According to the latest information from the Ukrainian military, it goes far beyond the use of Iranian-made Shahed drones.
In the early hours of 27 August, Ukrainian air defences shot down or neutralised 233 Russian targets in a single night-time bombardment. Among them were 258 attack drones, two Oniks anti-ship missiles and several Iskander-M and KN-23 ballistic missiles.
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, around a third of those drones are jet-powered, while the rest are a mix of Shahed-type drones, Gerbera systems and Banderol missiles, as well as decoys.
That mix gives a fairly accurate picture of the state of Russia’s unmanned arsenal at this stage of the war: it is no longer based on a single model but on a whole family of systems performing different roles, from flooding the sky with cheap swarms to punching through at more than 500 kilometres per hour.
Part of the explanation lies in cost. Firing a million-dollar interceptor at a drone worth between €25,000-40,000 (€21,000-35,000) is unsustainable in the long run and that imbalance is precisely what Moscow is exploiting by launching waves capable of exhausting far more expensive air-defence systems with its drones, as well as with more conventional weapons.
The bulk of this drone fleet comes from the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan, some 1,200 kilometres from the Ukrainian border. The complex covers more than 2.8 million square metres and it is estimated that around 15% of its facilities are devoted, directly or indirectly, to war production.
There, composite fuselages are moulded, engines are manufactured, onboard electronics are assembled and completed parts are stored.
Ukrainian strikes on the complex have forced Russia to move much of that chain underground.
A Ukrainian open-source analyst estimates that around 42,000 square metres of underground space have already been built at Alabuga, the equivalent of six football pitches.
According to Russian media cited by 'The Economist', daily production of Geran-2 drones already exceeds 100 units, with plans to reach 500 a day. Geran-2 drones are the systems better known as the Shahed-136.
In terms of overall volume, estimates vary by source but point in the same direction. The Centre for Strategic and International Studies calculated that in March 2026 Russia was producing around 5,500 drones a month, while Ukrainian military intelligence put August output at around 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones and some 2,800 Geran-2 a month.
In March of that same year, according to a report cited by Euronews, Russia had launched 6,462 Shahed-type drones and related attack and decoy systems, of which 4,186 were Shahed-type Geran-2 attack drones, an average of 208 launches a day – a pace that on some days rose to more than 900 drones .
This is the model that has underpinned most attacks since 2022. Designed in Iran, Russia manufactures its own version at Alabuga under the Geran-2 designation.
As Ukrainian interceptors have improved, Russia has been replacing propellers with jet engines. The leap has taken place in three stages.
The first, the Geran-3, based on the Shahed-238, reused the Geran-2 fuselage with an added turbojet. It reached speeds of between 300 and 370 km/h and had an operational range of close to 1,000 kilometres, with a combined thermal and fragmentation warhead of around 50 kilograms.
Ukrainian intelligence documented dozens of foreign components in its wreckage, many of them from US manufacturers, as well as Chinese and European parts.
The Geran-4 followed with an entirely redesigned fuselage rather than a simple adaptation. Its dimensions remain similar to those of the original Shahed – about 3.5 metres long with a 3-metre wingspan – but with integrated fixed wings to reduce drag.
According to specialist analysis, it cruises at between 300-350 km/h, with peaks of up to 500 km/h, flies at 4,000 to 5,000 metres and delivers a 50-kilogram warhead at a range of between 450 and 850 kilometres.
In practice, however, Russia has managed to stretch that figure: flying at high altitude to cut fuel consumption, a Geran-4 recorded a flight of around 960 kilometres on 28 August 2026, a distance that brings almost the whole of Ukrainian territory within range. Its cost is put at between $85,000-120,000 (€74,000-105,000) per unit.
The Geran-5 is the most recent variant. According to an analysis by the International Institute for Strategic Studies, it can reach up to 600 km/h, has a range of about 950 kilometres and a payload of around 90 kilograms; German-made transistors have been found in its remains . Both models are powered by the TF-TJ2000A engine.
The impact on Ukrainian defences has been significant. In March 2026 Ukraine was intercepting more than 90% of the drones launched against its territory ; by June, with Geran jet drones deployed on a large scale, that rate had fallen to just over 50%. Kyiv responded with its own jet-powered interceptors, such as the Alexa Spatium, which entered service on 21 August 2026.
Originally conceived as a cheap decoy to saturate radar screens alongside real Geran-2 drones, the Gerbera model has been steadily gaining its own offensive capability.
Unlike the Shahed and Geran drones, designed for long-range strikes, the Lancet is a short-range weapon intended to hit specific frontline targets such as artillery, radar systems or armoured vehicles.
It is worth noting that social networks have circulated claims of a variant called Lancet XXL, with a warhead equivalent to 20 kilograms of TNT and a range of 200 kilometres, powered by an internal combustion engine instead of the usual electric motor.
However, this version has not been officially confirmed either by ZALA Aero or by the Russian Defence Ministry.
This is not an attack drone but a reconnaissance platform whose main role is to correct artillery fire and monitor troop movements.
This is the most ambitious combat drone in the Russian arsenal, although serial production was slow to ramp up and it has never played as prominent a role as the Shaheds.
The latest development is not about range but about electromagnetic stealth. Because they are physically connected by cable to the operator , these drones emit no radio signal that can be jammed or detected.
The Russian army has a multitude of drones at its disposal and some of them have a range of up to 1,000 kilometres, which means that the CIA’s estimates may in fact underestimate the threat of a possible attack on Spain, France or Italy from the Mediterranean.
From a ship in the shadow fleet in the Mediterranean, the Russian army could launch Geran-2, Geran-3, Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones, all capable of carrying an explosive payload to targets at almost 1,000 kilometres.

NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV) - Metro Nashville is honoring the late Queen of Country on September 25, which has been officially declared Dolly Day.
The date is a play on her famous song “9 to 5,” and it’s meant to celebrate and remember her. Mayor Freddie O’Connell encouraged residents to wear pink and donate to local causes.
At 5 p.m., participating music venues will play live performances of “9 to 5” across the city. Some businesses will have Dolly-themed food and drink deals. And the Musicians Hall of Fame is donating $9.25 from each admission to the Imagination Library in honor of the holiday.
The celebration will close with fireworks in downtown Nashville starting at 9:25 p.m.
WSMV4 has rounded up a list of celebrations across the city. See the details below.
Here’s a list of Dolly Day events across Nashville, with details from event organizers:
The Metropolitan Nashville Airport Authority voted 6-0 this month to begin the process of modifying Nashville International Airport’s name in honor of Dolly Parton.
The authority said a final name has not yet been determined and that it will work with appropriate parties to decide how Parton’s name and legacy will be incorporated.
The decision begins a multifaceted process, with airport officials expecting to share more specific plans in the coming months.
A bench at Centennial Park now carries a “lasting tribute” to the late country legend and one of Tennessee’s most beloved icons.
Metro Parks and Centennial Park Conservancy have dedicated a bench near the Sunken Garden in memory of Dolly Parton.
The bench celebrates her and her “connection to the park, her contributions to the Nashville community and her lifelong commitment to inspiring children to read, dream and imagine.”
Dolly Parton’s estate is planning a music festival to honor the late Queen of Country Music.
Nashville has been selected as one of two cities in the world to host DOLLYFEST next year. The other location will be London, England, and the festivals will take place across “two consecutive weekends” in 2027.
“What was originally planned as a multi-artist event for January 2026 in Nashville and intended to feature Parton as performer and host, will now morph into a global double-day, double-weekend, double-continent party of a lifetime,” a press release on the event said.
The Grand Ole Opry hosted a sold-out, standing-room-only show to honor Dolly Parton.
Every artist who took the stage during the show had a tie to Parton.
Carly Pearce, who was invited to become an Opry member by Parton herself five years ago, was among the performers. Other artists included T. Graham Brown, Channing Wilson, Belle Frantz, Kathy Mattea, Molly Tuttle, Opry Square Dancers and Dan Tyminski.

The SEC gantlet begins for two of the conference’s top teams at Neyland Stadium. For Tennessee freshman quarterback Faizon Brandon, it’s about as difficult an introduction to conference play as he could get. At least he’s playing at home.

articles.title_orig: ‘We are hemorrhaging’: Cracks emerge in GOP’s Florida firewall
articles.title_zh: ‘We are hemorrhaging’: Cracks emerge in GOP’s Florida firewall
articles.content_orig:
Fox News Digital spoke to Donalds about his tightening race for Florida governor against Democrat David Jolly, a former Republican.
Florida gubernatorial candidate, Republican Congressman Byron Donalds , is taking aim at his Democratic opponent David Jolly over his shifting political positions and party affiliation, in a contest that is resurfacing themes from the 2016 congressional race between Jolly and Charlie Crist.
"You were pro-choice, then you were pro-life, then you were pro-choice. It was only after you switched parties that you switched your position. This was not a matter of conviction for you; it was for political convenience," Jolly said about Charlie Crist when Jolly was a Republican running against Crist, a Democrat, for Congress in 2016.
Ten years later, Jolly is now a Democrat running for Florida governor and facing the same criticism for allegedly changing his positions for political gain, this time, in his race for governor against Donalds.
"The shift in positions by David Jolly is not because of personal conviction, it is purely because of political convenience," Donalds told Fox News Digital, referencing that 2016 exchange.
DESANTIS ENDORSES FLORIDA GOP SLATE INCLUDING BYRON DONALDS IN GOVERNOR'S RACE
Rep. Byron Donalds, R-Fla., takes aim at gubernatorial opponent David Jolly's decades-long history of changing parties and political positions in an interview with Fox News Digital. (Eva Marie Uzcategui/Bloomberg via Getty Images ; Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
Some of the shifts in Jolly’s positions include issues like abortion, immigration and drilling off the coast of Florida.
As a Republican, Jolly said he believed "life begins at conception," authored legislation to defund Planned Parenthood and co-sponsored fetal-personhood legislation. He also voted for a federal 20-week abortion ban. Now running as a Democrat, Jolly calls himself "pro-choice," supports codifying the Roe v. Wade framework and says he would veto legislation restricting abortion access as governor.
Jolly’s immigration views have also shifted sharply as he attempts to run for governor in a state that voted for Trump each of the last three presidential cycles by wide margins, with many voters motivated by Trump’s immigration policies.
As a Republican, he campaigned on securing the border, supported tighter screening for Syrian and Iraqi refugees and voted for the American SAFE Act. Today, he says the country should have "wide gates" for people coming to work or seek asylum, argues that crossing the border without legal status should not necessarily be treated as a crime in those circumstances and has called the Republican link between immigration and crime "gross," "immoral" and "wrong."
As voters consistently say that affordability is a top-of-mind concern, Donalds is also hitting Jolly’s record on healthcare as an example of inconsistency that shows a lack of credibility on the issue.
NEVER-TRUMP REPUBLICAN IS TOP DEM CHOICE IN CRUCIAL FLORIDA PRIMARY
Former Republican Representative David Jolly, Democratic gubernatorial candidate for Florida, speaks during the National Action Network (NAN) 35th Anniversary Convention in New York on Thursday, April 9, 2026. (Victor J. Blue/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"When David Jolly was in Congress, he opposed Obamacare," Donalds said. "Now trying to run for governor, he wants to expand Obamacare in Florida. I mean, these are just some of the complete shifts that we've seen in what he stands for."
Another issue Donalds is taking issue with involves the period after the devastating Deepwater Horizon oil spill, which sent oil and tar balls washing ashore along roughly 178 miles of Florida coastline, contributed to an estimated loss of 1.88 million planned recreational visits in northwest Florida and cost the region $1.3 billion in visitor spending, $2.04 billion in economic output and more than 20,000 job-years.
Within a year of the spill, Jolly’s lobbying firm represented a client that publicly advocated for legislation that could have expanded offshore drilling in the Gulf of Mexico. Three Bridges Advisors listed H.R. 909, the Roadmap for America’s Energy Future, among the subjects of its 2011 lobbying activity for the Free Enterprise Nation, which supported the bill. Jolly also wrote a post on the group’s website stating that Free Enterprise Nation was "advocating for" the legislation.
BYRON DONALDS SHUTS DOWN BILL MAHER’S CLAIM ON GOP PRIMARY RACISM, SAYS 'FLORIDA IS A MERITOCRACY'
Rep. Byron Donalds, a Republican from Florida and gubernatorial candidate, won Florida's Republican primary for governor on Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026, in Orlando, Fla., easily fending off challengers after receiving an early endorsement from President Donald Trump. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Jolly said he had "never lobbied for offshore drilling," but PolitiFact rated that claim "Mostly False" after finding that Jolly acknowledged attending a meeting where the bill was discussed, which lobbying experts said technically counted as lobbying.
Donalds cited the controversy to Fox News Digital saying, "Deepwater Horizon exploded in the Gulf of America, David Jolly went and became a lobbyist for more oil drilling off the coast of Florida, that is a fact and so, what we're seeing is a history of somebody who does everything possible, will say whatever, will be paid by whomever that are only in the interest of David Jolly."
With polls showing a tightening race, the RealClearPolitics average gives Donalds a nearly 4-point lead. The candidates are also sparring over debate scheduling: Donalds has agreed to three proposed debates, while Jolly, who previously accepted two other debate invitations, has now ruled out participating in debates this cycle.
"Now he's ducking debates," Donalds told Fox News Digital. "He won't debate me because he knows that on a debate stage, I will hold him accountable for these things."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Jolly has hit Donalds on the campaign trail on a variety of issues as he tries to become the first Democrat to win a governor’s race in Florida since Lawton Chiles won re-election in 1994. Primarily, Jolly has focused on data centers and labeled Donalds as a candidate more interested in partisan culture-war battles than addressing Florida’s rising housing, insurance and healthcare costs.
Fox News Digital reached out to the Jolly campaign for comment.
Donalds told Fox News Digital that Jolly’s flips on both party registration and the issues are things his campaign will continue to focus on.
"What you find with David Jolly is somebody who's done a complete 180 simply to run for office again and to gain relevance again and the people of Florida simply cannot trust David Jolly because we cannot afford David Jolly’s flip-flopping when it comes to the great state of Florida," Donalds said.

articles.title_zh: Russia could attack a NATO country within months, Danish intelligence warns
articles.content_orig:
Danish intelligence officials have warned that Russia could launch a "limited" military attack against a NATO member in the coming months, saying the Kremlin appears more willing to take risks after more than 4½ years of war against Ukraine.
The Danish Defence Intelligence Service, or DDIS, on Thursday identified a "low but growing risk" that Russia could carry out isolated strikes with long-range weapons on infrastructure that is critical to the support of Ukraine.
"A limited military attack would be a desperate move on Russia's part and, like the intensified hybrid attacks, could potentially take place in the coming months," it wrote in a report.
"The purpose would be to redirect European resources away from supporting Ukraine and to sow division within NATO, should the alliance fail to agree on a collective response."
The DDIS added that it saw no indications that Russia would launch an outright invasion of a NATO country, although it said it could not rule this out.
Russia could also deploy a limited number of troops, possibly without national insignia, into NATO countries on its border, the DDIS said. However, it said that such a buildup would be difficult to conceal and take several months to prepare.
The new threat assessment joins a chorus of Russia warnings from top European security officials and lawmakers in recent days.
NATO members that border Russia are Finland, Norway and Poland as well as the Baltic states of Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania.
Poland's government on Thursday said a blaze at a Starlink ground station in the country was an act of sabotage aimed at disrupting internet services, including for Ukraine's military.
Poland's deputy prime minister, Krzysztof Gawkowski, said it had not yet been established who was responsible for the fire, but "many signs suggest this aligns with Russia's new ‌doctrine ⁠of attack," according to Reuters .
A spokesperson for Russia's embassy in London was not immediately available to comment when contacted by CNBC. The Kremlin has previously denied involvement in similar incidents.
Denmark's intelligence service also warned that Russia will intensify its hybrid war by carrying out more attacks against the West and NATO, "with greater consequences for the targeted countries than in the past."
These could include major cyberattacks that seriously damage vital societal functions as well as sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties, the DDIS said.
